### page_1
Geophys. J. R. astr. Soc. (1979) 59, 529-537
Mesozoic palaeomagnetism in Vestfjella, Dronning
Maud Land, East Antarctica
Reidar LdVfie
Department of Geophysics, University of Bergen,
N-5014 Bergen, Norway
Received 1979 April 30; in original form 1979 February 26
Summary. Thermal and alternating field demagnetization of oriented samples
of Mesozoic lava flows (200-230 Myr) and dykes (1 54-1 72 Myr) collected
from seven nunataks within the Vestfjella region, Dronning Maud Land,
revealed stable directions of magnetization of normal and reverse polarity.
Directional distributions of both polarities define tight groups along the same
palaeomagnetic axis. Depending on whether the regional westward dip of the
lava flows originated prior to, or after the intrusive igneous phase, two
or one, respectively, palaeomagnetic pole(s) can be estimated. Both poles,
however, are in general accord with previous Mesozoic poles from East
Antarctica.
Introduction and geological summary
Prior to this study, stability-tested palaeomagnetic results from East Antarctica were limited
to eight studies (McElhinny 1973), five of which represented investigations of Mesozoic
rocks exposed along the Transantarctic Mountains, The present study adds further palaeo-
magnetic information to this period by describing results of palaeomagnetic investigations of
Upper Triassic and Middle to Upper Jurassic igneous rocks from Vestfjella, Dronning Maud
Land.
Vestfjella is situated on an ice-covered peninsula extending into the Weddell Sea and con-
stitutes some of the northernmost exposures of the Transantarctic Mountains. It consists of
a large number of nunataks, rising up to 400m above the ice-cover, and extending in a
NNE-SSW direction for some 130 km. The dominant rock type is subaerial basaltic lava
flows, ranging in thickness from 1 to 25 m, dipping slightly to the WNW and building up a
sequence of estimated stratigraphic thickness of around 2500 m (Furnes & Mitchell 1978).
The lava flows are rather altered, reflected both by a greenish colour and the presence of an
assemblage of secondary minerals such as quartz, calcite, prehnite and epidote. Field evidence
suggests that this alteration, which apparently becomes more pronounced towards the base of
the succession, is due to syn- and/or post-volcanic hydrothermal activity (Furnes & Mitchell
1978). The lava pile is cut by a large number of steeply dipping basaltic dykes 0.5-10 m
in thickness. The strike is predominantly in a NW-SE direction, locally coinciding with the

estimated fold axis of the lava flows. This suggests that the dyke intrusions may have caused
the development of local low-amplitude folds (Hjelle & Winsnes 1972).
Apart from quartz and calcite filings in the contact zones, the dykes are fresh-looking and
17 K-Ar determinations (Fumes& Mitchell 1978) give ages ranging between 156 and 172 Myr
(Middle-Upper Jurassic). Four K-Ar ages of lava samples from the stratigraphically highest
sections range between 200 and 231 Myr (Upper Triassic) of which the youngest ages are
regarded as the most reliable ones (Furnes & Mitchell 1978).
Field work
Samples for this study were collected by a field party visiting Vestfjella during the Norwegian
Antarctic Expedition of 1976/77. A total of 200 oriented samples from 41 sites were
collected from the named nunataks in Fig. 1. In addition to standard hand sampling, a
portable drill was employed, by which more than half of the samples (126) were obtained.
Orientation by both Sun and magnetic compass was accomplished on 154 samples, giving an
arithmetic mean of the magnetic declination of 8.4" W (u = k 0.8"). The small scatter of the
mean suggests the absence of major local anomalies; hence the strike directions of samples
oriented by magnetic compass only are corrected by this mean declination.
Attempts to trace magnetic polarity transitions within the stratigraphically lowermost
section (Pagodromen) utilizing a portable flux-gate magnetometer, were not successful in
that no sample gave any detectable deflection. The altered and badly cracked surface con-
ditions put severe limitations on an effective sampling of the lava flows. Hence only 10 out
of 42 sites represent lava flows.
Magnetomineralogy
Properties ofthe magnetic minerals were investigated by ore microscopy and thermomagnetic
analysis (1, T). The opaque mineralogy in one polished section from each site was studied

### page_3
Mesozoic palaeomagnetism in Vestfjella 531
employing the magnetic colloid technique in order to detect and enhance the visibility of
intragrain magnetic structures.
The lava flows from Pagodromen (Fig. 1) differ from all the other samples in the almost
complete absence of visible opaque minerals even at the highest available magnification
(x 2100). In reflected light the ground mass is brightly coloured in yellow, green, brown
and red. Yellow-white structures are present which may represent relicts of titanomagnetite
in oxidation classes 11-VI. Low saturation magnetizations associated with predominantly
hyperbolic thermomagnetic curves reflect major contributions from paramagnetic minerals
although minor inflexion points around 560-580°C suggest the presence of small quantities
of almost pure magnetite. Macrocrysts of prehnite coated with epidote reflect hydrothermal
alterations at high pressures and temperatures (Ade-Hall, Palmer & Hubbard 1971), probably
accounting for the dissolution of the deuteric crystallized magnetic minerals. The mineralogy
in the four additional lava flows situated at higher stratigraphic levels (Kjakebeinet, Nunatak
A and Muren) resemble the intrusive rocks with the exception that sulphide is absynt.
The intrusive rocks generally have major mineralogical features in common. The opaque
mineralogy is dominated by skeletal to euhedral titanomagnetite grains (5-100~) in high
temperature oxidation classes 1-111 (Ade-Hall et al. 1971). Low temperature alteration
features such as maghemitization and granulation cover between 10-80 per cent of the
grain surfaces. Non-magnetic cubic sulphides (< lop) in addition to slightly altered separate
ilmenite rods amounts to less than 25 per cent of the opaque minerals.
Thermomagnetic analyses reveal a range of features reflecting different degrees of low-
temperature alterations of the titanomagnetites. The J, - T curves are all irreversible with
single initial Curie temperatures between 520 and 580"C, decreasing by 20-40°C after
heating to 700"C, associated with either an increase or a decrease of the saturation magne-
tization. A feature resembling the 'kink' described by Ade-Hall et al. (1971), is present in
about 10 per cent of the samples. Ade-Hall et al. believe this to be ascribed to a combination
of high degree deuteric and hydrothermal alteration.
Demagnetization experiments
One cylinder (19 x 19mm) prepared from each sample was subjected to progressive alter-
nating field (&,= = 1000 Oe) and/or thermal demagnetization treatment. The direction and
intensity of remanent magnetization was measured with a commercial slow-speed spinner
magnetometer, and magnetic susceptibility was determined with a commercial low field
inductance bridge. Results of the demagnetization treatment can be divided into three cate-
gories:
(1) Systematic directional trends terminating in stable end points defined as a cluster
of at least three consecutive directions less than 5" of arc apart were found in 159 samples.
Median destructive fields range from 150 to 400 Oe and are associated with a smooth decay
of the remanent intensity. At the highest temperatures or peak alternating-fields the
magnetization vector sometimes starts moving out from the stable end point groups in an
erratic fashion. In order to retrieve palaeomagnetic information, great circles were fitted
to the directional trends by a least-squares method (Halls 1976), and the intersection points
of converging great circles satisfying adopted selection criteria (Halls 1976) were analysed.
However, no unique intersection point deviating from the distribution of stable end points
was found.
(2) Af-treatment proved unsuccessful in demagnetizing the remanence in samples from
five dykes from Pagodromen, Steinkjeften and Kjakebeinet. The NRM directions remained
stable even after treatment in fields of lOOOOe, after which 45 per cent of the remanence

intensity remained. Subsequent thermal demagnetization on top of the af treatment accom-
plished complete demagnetization of these specimens. On this procedure the remanent
directions in samples from Kjakebeinet and Steinkjeften remained stable while the Pago-
dromen samples revealed a rather peculiar behaviour, demonstrated in Fig. 2. Above c.
400°C a rapid directional change takes place associated with a drop in the intensities and
a pronounced increase in the susceptibilities measured after each heating step. The direc-
tional trends describe arcs of almost 180". In some cases (cx Fig. 2, VF78 and VF86), the
directions, upon further heat treatment may turn back towards the initial directions.
Although no stable antiparallel groups can be defined the directional behaviour, seen in
conjunction with the distinct jump in the susceptibilities, tentatively suggest a case of
partial self-reversal caused by magnetomineralogical changes (Creer 197 1) induced during
thermal treatment. Neither ore microscopy nor thermomagnetic studies could reveal signifi-
cant differences between heated and unheated samples which contained titanomagnetite
grains with more than 30 per cent granulation. Alternatively, these results could also reflect
the presence of two opposed remanent directions, deviating significantly from being anti-
parallel. The pronounced increase in the susceptibility above 400°C could reflect the break-
down of mineral phases carrying the prevailing normal magnetization thus uncovering an
overprint of reversed polarity.

(3) Systematic directional trends, encountered at the lower demagnetization levels in
20 samples, were succeeded by a scattered behaviour associated with a greater than 70 per
cent reduction of the intensities. No stable end points were obtained and analyses of con-
verging great circles fitted to the smoother fraction of the trends, was not successful in
defining any unique intersection points.
Palaeomagnetic directions
From demagnetization of 194 samples 174 gave stable end points. 32 of these directions
(nine sites) were excluded from the final palaeomagnetic results adopting the following
selection criteria:
(1) Each site should be represented by more than three stable end points and (2) site
mean scatter (ag5s)h ould be less than 30". Four sites were excluded on the grounds given
in (1) and five due to (2).
Fig. 3 shows the remaining 142 stable directions plotted separately for each nunatak.
Site mean directions and relevant statistical parameters are presented in Table 1. The
directions, deviating significantly from the present geomagnetic field axis, are clustered in
two almost antiparallel distributions. The normal polarity group has the highest concen-
tration of results and appears to have a slightly steeper inclination than the reversed one.
Apart from large differences in the within site scatter, attributed to a combination of
orientation effects and unsuccessful removal of deviating secondary components, only site
25 (Nunatak A) exhibits a somewhat anomalous distribution of stable directions. Collected
across a 3-m thick dyke, the seven samples define two significantly different groups, 25A

and 25B (cf. Fig. 3). The former (four samples) coincides with the general normal distri-
butions while the latter, a tightly clustered group of three directions, has a dip some 20"
shallower than the former. The deviating distribution consists of samples collected from
within 40cm of the western contact, as opposed to the more central positions of site 25A
samples, suggesting that the more rapid cooling rate of the contact zone may have provided
the necessary conditions for inducing a spot reading of the geomagnetic field during the
initial cooling of the igneous body.
The oldest lavas, sampled from the base of Pagodromen (sites 1-4), all have reversed
polarity as opposed to the stratigraphically younger lava flows (sites 13, 14 and 26). The
absence of both sedimentary and erosional surfaces within the lava pile (Furnes & Mitchell
1978) reflect a rather continuous emplacement of the lava flows during which at least one
reversal of the geomagnetic field took place. The palaeomagnetic polarity time scale for the
time interval in question (200-300 Myr) includes some 17 episodes of reversed polarity
(McElhinny & Burek 1971), allowing for a rather rapid accumulation of the lava succession.
Within the time range for the intrusive igneous activity (156-172Myr), only one reversed
epoch (Mateke zone, around 170Myr) has been recognized (McElhinny & Burek 1971),
implying that the reversely polarized dykes were intruded during the early stage of the
intrusive activity.

have not been subjected to any tectonic correction. Separate mean directions for lavas and
dykes, irrespective of polarity, are presented in Table 2. The almost coinciding directions

suggests an origin of the regional dip that post-dates the intrusive activity. The onset of sea
floor spreading off Dronning Maud Land around 150 Myr ago (Bergh 1977) post-dates the
intrusive episode in Vestfjella, and may thus represent the tectonic process resulting in the
regional inclination of the lava flows. The fairly low precision (high ag5)o f the palaeo-
magnetic results from the lava sites, compared to that of the dykes, can probably be
accounted for by the influence of local folds within the lavas, which originated during the
intrusive episode (Hjelle & Winsnes 1972), and by the unsuccessful removal of magnetic
components of opposite polarity.
Although the tectonic relationship between the nunataks are rather uncertain and the
slight dip of the lava flows varies within each region, an overall bedding correction for a
dip of I5"WNW is considered to be representative. The combined mean direction of all
sites, corrected for tectonism, and the corresponding pole positions are presented in Table
2.
Previous Mesozoic palaeomagnetic poles from East Antarctica are plotted in Fig. 4 in
addition to the pole positions from Vestfjella; 6A and 6B; prior to and after tectonic
correction respectively. Both poles are seen to fall within the general group of the previous
poles. However, the uncorrected pole 6A, (cJ Table 2) is in perfect agreement with the
suggested best estimate of the mean Mesozoic pole for East Antarctica (54" S, 154" W;
Beck 1972). This could either be coincidental, or imply that the tilting of the lava pile
pre-dates the intrusive phase. In this latter situation tilt correction should be applied to the
lava rocks only. Considering the almost coinciding mean directions of the lavas and dykes,
the corrected and uncorrected pole positions can be regarded as representative of the lavas
and the dykes respectively.
Although the scatter between the pole positions in Fig. 4 can be accounted for by the
expected behaviour of poles within the quasistatic interval for Gondwanaland (Briden 1967)
covering.the time span in question, the lower latitude of the tilt corrected, oldest pole, 6,,
is tentatively suggested to reflect the trend of a general decrease in latitude of palaeomagnetic
poles with increasing age. Thus, the two distinctly different pole positions 6~ (dykes) and
6, (lavas), would represent Middle/Upper Jurassic and Upper Triassic poles respectively.
In conclusion it should be stressed that the validity of the uncorrected pole, 6 ~de,pe nd
on an origin of the regional dip pre-dating the intrusive phase.
